I think that played a very small role. What you're talking about there is Community Reinvestment Act. Note that act specifically states that banks are not required to make high-risk loans that may result in losses. There was also no enforcement mechanism or penalty aside from the fact that compliance was taken into account for banks seeking to expand through mergers and acquisitions. This has also been a law since 1977.

I think one of the biggest issues is that banks were fraudulently rating the securities that were created by bundling these loans. The banks knew full well that in many cases those loans stood close to a 0% chance of ever being paid off, yet the securities made up of bundles of these loans were rated as maximally safe. Those securities were then used in a wide array of other investments. The logic was supposed to be that the loans failing was no problem since the housing market was so hot, they could just continue to resell the repossessed home for even more. Remember all those 'house flipping' shows just before the market crash suggesting the same? House prices were rapidly increasing, even in real cost, to be far outside the available income of most of anybody - but to justify their leveraging these unsafe loans they disingenuously kept with the assumption that the price could keep going higher and higher indefinitely. The complete lack of regulation enabled the banks to effectively make up their own rules as they went along.

The underlying loans crashing isn't what caused the huge crash. It was the fact that house of cards built up on top of these loans then came tumbling down on top. If the house of cards had never been built, then there would have been no major crash.
